chapter: Chemical Reactions and Equations (Class 10 Science, CBSE)
note: Authored MCQs, 40 per concept, 14 Easy / 13 Medium / 13 Hard. Options kept parallel in length so no key is identifiable by size alone.

2730.stem: Balancing an equation by adjusting coefficients one at a time is known as
2730.explanation: The hit-and-trial method, also called balancing by inspection, adjusts coefficients until every element matches.

options.why: That method balances redox half-equations using electrons.
That method balances redox equations using changes in oxidation state.
No graphical method is used for balancing equations.

2730.stem: In the hit-and-trial method, the numbers that may be changed are the
2730.explanation: Only coefficients, the numbers written in front of formulae, may be adjusted.

options.why: Changing a subscript makes it a different substance.
Atomic numbers are fixed properties of the elements.
Valencies determine the formulae and are not adjustable.

2730.stem: Hit-and-trial balancing is complete when
2730.explanation: Balancing is finished when every element has the same number of atoms on both sides.

options.text: every element matches on both sides

options.why: Appearance is not the test; atom counts are.
Coefficients in a balanced equation are usually different.
Coefficients remain in almost every balanced equation.

2730.stem: The hit-and-trial method is also known as balancing by
2730.explanation: Because the coefficients are found by looking at the atom counts, the method is also called balancing by inspection.

options.why: Titration is an experimental technique for finding concentration.
Substitution is an algebraic technique, not the standard name here.
Elimination is an algebraic technique for solving equations.

2730.stem: Which of these is NOT a step in hit-and-trial balancing?
2730.explanation: Changing a subscript is forbidden, because it replaces the substance with a different one.

options.why: Counting is the first step of every balancing attempt.
Adjusting coefficients is exactly what the method does.
Rechecking is essential once the coefficients are set.

2730.stem: The final coefficients of a balanced equation should be
2730.explanation: Convention requires the smallest set of whole numbers that balances the equation.

options.why: Any multiple balances, but convention prefers the smallest.
Fractions are cleared before the equation is final.
Most equations need coefficients greater than one.

2730.stem: Balancing H2 + Cl2 -> HCl requires the coefficient of HCl to be
2730.explanation: One hydrogen molecule and one chlorine molecule give two molecules of hydrogen chloride.

options.why: One molecule accounts for only one of each atom, not two.
Three would need more atoms than the reactants supply.
Four is twice the smallest whole-number answer.

2730.stem: In hit-and-trial balancing, the first thing to do is
2730.explanation: Listing the number of atoms of each element on both sides shows immediately what needs adjusting.

options.text: list the atoms on each side

options.why: A count makes the first choice informed rather than blind.
States are added after balancing is complete.
Conditions are added above the arrow at the end.

2730.stem: Balance Na + Cl2 -> NaCl. The coefficient of Na is
2730.explanation: Two chlorine atoms need two sodium atoms, giving 2Na + Cl2 -> 2NaCl.

options.why: One sodium atom leaves one chlorine atom unaccounted for.
Three sodium atoms exceed what the chlorine can combine with.
Four is twice the smallest whole-number answer.

2730.stem: Why is the method called hit-and-trial?
2730.explanation: Coefficients are tried and checked in turn until every element balances, so the answer is reached by trying rather than by formula.

options.text: Coefficients are tried and checked in turn
The formulae are guessed at random
options.why: Formulae must be correct before balancing begins.

options.text: The products are chosen by trial
options.why: The products are fixed before the equation is balanced.
The final answer is checked and certain.

2730.stem: A balanced equation has coefficients 2, 2, 1. Multiplying all by two gives
2730.explanation: The equation stays balanced but is no longer in the smallest whole-number form that convention requires.

options.why: Uniform multiplication always preserves the balance.
The substances are unchanged, so the reaction is the same.
The smaller set is the preferred one.

2730.stem: In hit-and-trial balancing, a fractional coefficient is
2730.explanation: A fraction may appear during the work but must be cleared by multiplying everything before the answer is final.

options.text: allowed during work, cleared at the end

options.why: Fractions are a useful intermediate step in many equations.
Convention requires whole numbers in the finished equation.

options.text: a sign of a wrong formula
options.why: Fractions arise routinely in correct equations.

2730.stem: Balance Mg + O2 -> MgO. The coefficient of MgO is
2730.explanation: Two oxygen atoms need two magnesium atoms, giving two units of magnesium oxide.

options.why: One unit uses only one oxygen atom, leaving one over.
Three units need three oxygen atoms, which O2 cannot supply.
Four is twice the smallest whole-number answer.

2730.stem: The hit-and-trial method works for school equations because those equations
2730.explanation: School equations involve few species, so the atom counts can be reconciled by inspection without algebra.

options.why: They need balancing, which is why the method is taught.
Coefficients are what the method supplies.
Every real reaction conserves mass.

2730.stem: Balance C2H6 + O2 -> CO2 + H2O. The coefficient of CO2 is
2730.explanation: Two C2H6 molecules supply four carbon atoms, so four molecules of carbon dioxide form.

options.why: Two would account for the carbon of only one C2H6 molecule.
Three does not match any whole-number set for this equation.
Six is the coefficient for water, not carbon dioxide.

2730.stem: Balancing Al + H2SO4 -> Al2(SO4)3 + H2 is quickest if the sulphate is treated as
2730.explanation: The sulphate group passes across unchanged, so counting it as one unit removes four oxygen counts from the work.

options.why: Correct but needlessly laborious when the group survives whole.
The sulphate is transferred, not merely present.
It must be balanced like everything else.

2730.stem: After balancing, a student has coefficients 2, 3, 1, 3 but finds hydrogen unequal. The correct action is to
2730.explanation: Balancing is not finished until every element matches, so the coefficients must be revised rather than accepted.

options.why: An unequal element means the equation is not balanced.
Changing a subscript alters the substance involved.
Hydrogen genuinely takes part and cannot be dropped.

2730.stem: Balance Fe2O3 + C -> Fe + CO2. The coefficient of C is
2730.explanation: Two Fe2O3 units carry six oxygen atoms, which form three CO2 molecules, so three carbon atoms are needed.

options.why: Two carbon atoms give only four oxygen atoms in the products.
Four carbon atoms would need eight oxygen atoms.
One carbon atom gives only two oxygen atoms in the product.

2730.stem: Which order of balancing C3H8 + O2 -> CO2 + H2O needs the least rework?
2730.explanation: Carbon and hydrogen are each confined to one compound on each side, so settling them first leaves only oxygen to total.

options.why: Oxygen would be disturbed by every later adjustment.
Starting with oxygen forces repeated revision.
Placing oxygen before carbon causes avoidable rework.

2730.stem: Balance KClO3 -> KCl + O2 using hit-and-trial. The coefficient of KClO3 is
2730.explanation: Two units give six oxygen atoms, which form three O2 molecules, so the whole-number set is 2, 2, 3.

options.why: One unit gives three oxygen atoms, which is not a whole number of O2.
Three units give nine oxygen atoms, again not a whole number of O2.
Four is twice the smallest whole-number answer.

2730.stem: Balance Ca3N2 + H2O -> Ca(OH)2 + NH3. The coefficient of H2O is
2730.explanation: One Ca3N2 gives three Ca(OH)2 and two NH3, needing six oxygen and twelve hydrogen atoms, which six water molecules supply.

options.why: Three water molecules supply only three oxygen atoms, not six.
Two water molecules cannot supply the six oxygen atoms needed.
Nine water molecules supply more oxygen than the products hold.

2730.stem: A student balances an equation and gets every coefficient as an even number. Before finishing, they should
2730.explanation: All-even coefficients share a common factor of two, so dividing through gives the smaller standard form.

options.why: Multiplying moves further from the smallest form.

options.text: leave the answer as it is
options.why: Convention requires the smallest whole-number set.
Changing a single coefficient would unbalance the equation.

2730.stem: Balance Zn + NaOH -> Na2ZnO2 + H2. The coefficient of NaOH is
2730.explanation: Two sodium atoms are needed for Na2ZnO2, and the two hydroxide groups supply the oxygen and the hydrogen molecule.

options.why: One supplies only one sodium atom, not the two required.
Three supplies three sodium atoms, one too many.
Four is twice the smallest whole-number answer.

2730.stem: Why does hit-and-trial balancing always terminate for a real reaction?
2730.explanation: Atoms are conserved, so a consistent whole-number solution must exist and can always be found by inspection.

options.text: The method is guaranteed by algebra
options.why: Algebra can be used, but that is a different method.
Equations may involve many elements and still balance.
No upper limit applies to coefficients.

2730.stem: Balance NH3 + O2 -> NO + H2O. The coefficient of O2 is
2730.explanation: Four NH3 give four NO and six H2O, needing ten oxygen atoms, which five O2 molecules supply.

options.why: Three molecules give six oxygen atoms, not the ten required.
Four molecules give eight oxygen atoms, still two short.
Six molecules give twelve oxygen atoms, two too many.

2730.stem: In hit-and-trial balancing, rechecking every element at the end is necessary because
2730.explanation: A coefficient change affects every element in that formula, so an element settled earlier can easily be disturbed.

options.why: Elements never change identity in a reaction.
The arrow is not altered during balancing.
There is a concrete reason, not merely a convention.

2730.stem: Balance MnO2 + Al -> Mn + Al2O3. The coefficient of Al is
2730.explanation: Three MnO2 units carry six oxygen atoms, which form two Al2O3, so four aluminium atoms are needed.

options.why: Two aluminium atoms form only one Al2O3, using three oxygen atoms.
Three aluminium atoms cannot form a whole number of Al2O3.
Six aluminium atoms need nine oxygen atoms, more than available.

2730.stem: A student cannot balance an equation after repeated attempts. The most likely cause is that
2730.explanation: Any equation with correct formulae can be balanced, so persistent failure points to a wrong formula.

options.why: Occurrence is a separate matter from balancing on paper.
Every real reaction conserves atoms and so balances.
Reversing the arrow changes no atom count.

2730.stem: Why is hit-and-trial inadequate for a complicated redox equation in solution?
2730.explanation: Electrons and ionic charge must also balance, which inspection of atom counts alone cannot achieve.

options.text: Charge must balance as well as atoms

options.why: Redox equations have products like any other.

options.text: Atoms are not conserved in redox
options.why: Atoms are conserved in every chemical reaction.
Redox equations balance with whole numbers too.

2730.stem: Two correct balancings of one equation differ by a factor of three. This shows the method determines
2730.explanation: Balancing fixes the ratios of the substances, not their absolute numbers, so any uniform multiple is also balanced.

options.why: No absolute count is implied by an equation.
Masses need molar masses in addition to coefficients.
Rate is never conveyed by an equation.

2730.stem: In balancing, leaving a free element until last is justified because its coefficient
2730.explanation: A free element contains only one kind of atom, so changing its coefficient cannot disturb any other element's count.

options.why: Free elements often carry coefficients above one.
It must balance like every other species.
The subscript is fixed; the coefficient is what is chosen.

2730.stem: A balanced equation is multiplied by 1.5 throughout. The result is
2730.explanation: The ratios are preserved so it is still balanced, but some coefficients are now fractional and must be cleared.

options.why: Uniform multiplication always preserves the balance.
The substances are untouched by multiplication.
The standard form uses the smallest whole numbers.

2730.stem: Which criticism of hit-and-trial as a method is fairest?
2730.explanation: It is reliable but unsystematic, so it gives no guarantee about how long the work will take on a complex equation.

options.text: It is reliable but not systematic
It gives the wrong answer often
options.why: A checked answer from this method is correct.
Only coefficients are touched, never the formulae.
It balances school equations routinely.

2730.stem: A student balances by algebra and gets the same answer as hit-and-trial. This is expected because
2730.explanation: Both methods solve the same system of atom-conservation constraints, so the smallest whole-number solution is unique.

options.why: Algebra is exact and gives the same result.
They are genuinely identical, not merely similar.
Coefficients are determined, not arbitrary.

2730.stem: Why can balancing never reveal that a written reaction does not actually occur?
2730.explanation: Balancing tests only whether atoms are conserved on paper, which any invented but well-formed equation can satisfy.

options.why: It offers no test of reality at all.
Many balanced equations describe reactions that never occur.
It does not test formulae either; a wrong formula can still balance.

2730.stem: An equation with eight species is being balanced by inspection. The best way to keep control is to
2730.explanation: Working from the most constrained element to the least, and recording the counts as you go, prevents the oscillation that wastes most of the time.

options.text: work from most constrained to least

options.why: Free elements are disturbed by every later change.
Letters bear no relation to the constraints.
Simultaneous guessing gives no way to correct errors.

2730.stem: A student changes O2 to O3 to make an equation balance. The deepest objection is that
2730.explanation: Ozone is a different substance from oxygen, so the balanced equation now describes a reaction that was never carried out.

options.text: the equation still will not balance
options.why: The objection stands even where the counts do work out.

options.text: three is not a valid subscript
options.why: Three is a perfectly valid subscript in other formulae.
No such limit exists on coefficients.

2730.stem: Why does convention insist on the smallest whole-number coefficients rather than any balanced set?
2730.explanation: A single agreed form makes equations directly comparable and makes calculations reproducible between chemists.

options.text: One agreed form keeps results comparable
Larger sets are not really balanced
options.why: Larger uniform multiples are perfectly balanced.

options.text: Small numbers are easier to multiply
options.why: Convenience is minor beside comparability.
Conservation holds at any uniform scale.

2730.stem: An equation balances with coefficients 1, 1, 1, 1 on the first attempt. A student suspects an error. The best judgement is that
2730.explanation: Some reactions genuinely balance with unit coefficients, so this is no evidence of a mistake by itself.

options.why: Unit coefficients occur in many correct equations.
No such requirement exists.
A correct balanced equation needs no rewriting.

2730.stem: What does the reliability of hit-and-trial balancing tell us about chemical change?
2730.explanation: That a whole-number solution always exists reflects the fact that matter is made of discrete atoms that are conserved.

options.text: Matter is made of discrete conserved atoms

options.why: Randomness would give no consistent whole-number solution.
Mass is conserved, which is why balancing works.
Atoms are not divided in chemical reactions.

2731.stem: In a chemical equation, the symbol (s) after a formula means the substance is
2731.explanation: The symbol (s) stands for solid.

options.why: A solution in water is shown by (aq).
A gas is shown by (g).
A pure liquid is shown by (l).

2731.stem: The symbol (aq) written after a formula means the substance is
2731.explanation: The symbol (aq) means aqueous, that is, dissolved in water.

options.why: A pure liquid is shown by (l), not (aq).
A solid is shown by (s).
A gas is shown by (g) whatever is beneath it.

2731.stem: Which symbol shows that a substance is a gas?
2731.explanation: The symbol (g) placed after the formula shows the substance is a gas.

options.why: This stands for solid.
This stands for pure liquid.
This stands for aqueous solution.

2731.stem: In 2H2O(l) -> 2H2(g) + O2(g), the reactant is
2731.explanation: Water carries the symbol (l), so it is present as a pure liquid.

options.why: The products carry (g); the reactant carries (l).
No (s) appears anywhere in this equation.
No (aq) appears anywhere in this equation.

2731.stem: State symbols are added to an equation mainly to
2731.explanation: They say what will actually be seen, such as a solid settling out or a gas bubbling off.

options.why: Balance depends only on atom counts.
The formulae already identify every substance.
Rate is never shown in an equation.

2731.stem: In BaCl2(aq) + Na2SO4(aq) -> BaSO4(s) + 2NaCl(aq), the precipitate is
2731.explanation: Barium sulphate carries (s), which marks it as the insoluble solid that separates out.

options.why: Sodium chloride carries (aq), so it stays dissolved.
This is a reactant and carries (aq).
This is a reactant and carries (aq).

2731.stem: The difference between (l) and (aq) is that (aq) means
2731.explanation: The symbol (aq) means dissolved in water, whereas (l) means the pure substance itself is liquid.

options.why: Temperature is not indicated by state symbols.
Viscosity is not indicated by state symbols.
Molten sodium chloride is (l) but dissolved sodium chloride is (aq).

2731.stem: In Zn(s) + 2HCl(aq) -> ZnCl2(aq) + H2(g), the substance that bubbles off is
2731.explanation: Hydrogen carries (g), so it leaves the mixture as a gas.

options.why: Zinc carries (s) and is the solid metal used up.
The acid carries (aq) and stays in solution.
Zinc chloride carries (aq) and stays dissolved.

2731.stem: State symbols are written
2731.explanation: Each symbol is placed immediately after the formula it describes, in brackets.

options.why: Conditions such as heat go above the arrow.
The position before a formula is used for coefficients.

options.text: at the end of the equation
options.why: Each substance needs its own symbol in its own place.

2731.stem: Which state symbol would molten iron carry?
2731.explanation: Molten iron is the pure element in the liquid state, so it carries (l).

options.why: Iron is not dissolved in water when it is molten.
Molten means it is no longer solid.
Iron vapour would be (g), but molten iron is liquid.

2731.stem: In CaCO3(s) -> CaO(s) + CO2(g), the escaping product is
2731.explanation: Carbon dioxide carries (g) and so leaves the vessel, while both solids remain.

options.why: Calcium oxide carries (s) and stays behind.
This is the reactant and carries (s).
The (g) symbol marks a product that leaves as a gas.

2731.stem: Adding state symbols to a balanced equation changes
2731.explanation: State symbols add information about what is observed and leave the atom counts untouched.

options.why: Symbols in brackets carry no atoms.
The formulae are unchanged.
The arrow is unchanged.

2731.stem: Which of these would carry the symbol (aq)?
2731.explanation: Dilute sulphuric acid is the substance dissolved in water, so it is aqueous.

options.why: An undissolved solid carries (s).
A gas carries (g).
A pure liquid carries (l).

2731.stem: The full form of the symbol (aq) is
2731.explanation: The abbreviation stands for aqueous, from the Latin for water.

options.why: This is an ordinary English word, unrelated to state symbols.
This is not a chemical term at all.
This is not a chemical term at all.

2731.stem: Adding state symbols to Pb(NO3)2 + 2KI -> PbI2 + 2KNO3 gives PbI2 as
2731.explanation: Lead iodide is insoluble and appears as a yellow precipitate, so it carries (s).

options.why: Lead iodide is insoluble, so it does not stay in solution.
Lead iodide is a solid, not a gas.
It is not a pure liquid; it separates as a solid.

2731.stem: Why is it wrong to write NaCl(l) for salt dissolved in water?
2731.explanation: The symbol (l) means molten pure salt at over 800 degrees Celsius, whereas dissolved salt is (aq).

options.why: Any pure liquid substance may carry (l).

options.text: salt can never be a liquid
options.why: Salt melts and is then genuinely (l).
They describe two quite different physical situations.

2731.stem: In 2H2(g) + O2(g) -> 2H2O(l), writing the product as (g) instead would imply
2731.explanation: It would mean steam was formed, which happens only above the boiling point of water.

options.why: A product is shown either way, so a reaction occurred.
State symbols do not affect the atom counts.
Water is not described as dissolved in water.

2731.stem: State symbols help predict which product can be separated by filtration, namely the one marked
2731.explanation: Only an insoluble solid, marked (s), can be caught on a filter paper.

options.why: A dissolved substance passes straight through the filter.
A gas escapes rather than being filtered.
A pure liquid passes through the filter paper.

2731.stem: A student writes CO2(aq) for the gas bubbling out of a fizzy drink being opened. The better symbol is
2731.explanation: Gas escaping from the liquid is no longer dissolved, so it should be marked (g).

options.why: The gas has left the solution, so it is no longer aqueous.
Carbon dioxide is not solid at room temperature.
Carbon dioxide is not a liquid at ordinary pressure.

2731.stem: In NaOH(aq) + HCl(aq) -> NaCl(aq) + H2O(l), no product can be filtered off because
2731.explanation: Neither product is marked (s), so nothing insoluble has formed and there is nothing to catch.

options.why: Neither product carries (g) in this equation.
Neutralisation certainly occurs, releasing heat.
Filtration separates insoluble solids, not gases.

2731.stem: Which state symbol should be written for the calcium hydroxide formed when quick lime is added to plenty of water?
2731.explanation: Calcium hydroxide is slightly soluble, so with plenty of water it is written (aq) as lime water.

options.why: It is dissolved in water rather than being a pure liquid.
Calcium hydroxide is not a gas.
With plenty of water enough dissolves to be written aqueous.

2731.stem: State symbols in an equation for electrolysis of molten sodium chloride would show NaCl as
2731.explanation: Molten means the pure salt is liquid, so it carries (l) and not (aq).

options.why: Molten salt contains no water at all.
Molten means it is no longer solid.
Sodium chloride vapour would need far higher temperatures.

2731.stem: Why do state symbols matter for predicting whether a double displacement will be visible?
2731.explanation: A visible change needs a product marked (s) or (g); if every product is (aq) nothing can be seen.

options.text: A visible change needs an (s) or (g) product
They show the colour of the products
options.why: Colour is not conveyed by a state symbol.

options.text: They show how fast the change is
options.why: Rate is not conveyed by an equation.
Balance depends only on atom counts.

2731.stem: In Fe(s) + CuSO4(aq) -> FeSO4(aq) + Cu(s), the substance depositing on the nail is
2731.explanation: Copper carries (s), so it forms as a solid deposit on the iron.

options.why: Iron sulphate carries (aq) and stays in solution.
This is a reactant and carries (aq).
Iron is the reactant being used up, not the deposit.

2731.stem: Omitting state symbols from an equation makes it
2731.explanation: The equation remains chemically correct and balanced but says less about what would actually be observed.

options.why: State symbols play no part in balancing.
It still uses formulae, so it remains a chemical equation.
Equations are frequently written without state symbols.

2731.stem: A precipitate and an escaping gas in the same reaction would be shown by the symbols
2731.explanation: The precipitate takes (s) and the escaping gas takes (g).

options.why: Neither of these marks a precipitate or an escaping gas.
A pure liquid is not an escaping gas.
An aqueous product is dissolved, not a precipitate.

2731.stem: Which pair of state symbols would tell you a reaction can be done in a test tube with no lid?
2731.explanation: If all species are (aq) or (s), nothing escapes and no lid is needed.

options.why: A gaseous product would escape from an open tube.
A gaseous product would escape from an open tube.
A gaseous product would escape from an open tube.

2731.stem: Why is (aq) not simply a special case of (l)?
2731.explanation: An aqueous species is dissolved and surrounded by water molecules, often as separate ions, whereas (l) describes the pure substance as a liquid.

options.text: An aqueous species is dissolved, often as ions
An aqueous species is always hotter
options.why: Temperature is not part of either symbol's meaning.

options.text: An aqueous species has no formula
options.why: Aqueous species have formulae like everything else.

options.text: They are in fact the same symbol
options.why: They describe two different physical situations.

2731.stem: Two equations for one reaction differ only in state symbols. The best conclusion is that
2731.explanation: They describe the same chemistry under different conditions, since state depends on temperature and on how much water is present.

options.text: one of them must be wrong
options.why: Both can be right for different temperatures.
The substances and the change are identical.
They carry real information about conditions.

2731.stem: A student writes AgCl(aq) as the product of mixing silver nitrate and sodium chloride solutions. The error matters because
2731.explanation: Silver chloride is insoluble, so marking it (aq) hides the white precipitate that is the whole observable result.

options.text: it hides the precipitate that forms

options.why: State symbols do not affect the atom counts.
Its formula, AgCl, is perfectly standard.
Nitrate is very commonly aqueous.

2731.stem: Why can the correct state symbol for a substance change between two experiments?
2731.explanation: State depends on temperature, pressure and whether water is present, all of which vary with the conditions used.

options.text: State depends on the conditions used

options.why: Identity is fixed by the formula.
They are determined by the physical situation.
Any substance can change state.

2731.stem: Which argument best defends including state symbols in every school equation?
2731.explanation: They connect the symbols on the page to what the student will actually see in the test tube, which is the point of the experiment.

options.text: They link the equation to the observation
They are needed to balance atoms
options.why: Balance depends only on atom counts.
They make the equation slightly longer.
The formulae already do that.

2731.stem: An equation shows every species as (aq). The strongest prediction about the observation is that
2731.explanation: With no solid or gas formed, any evidence of reaction must be something like a colour change or a temperature change.

options.text: no solid or gas will appear

options.why: A precipitate would be marked (s).
A gas would be marked (g).
Neutralisation occurs with all species aqueous.

2731.stem: Why does marking a product (g) have practical consequences for measuring conservation of mass?
2731.explanation: A gaseous product will escape from an open vessel, so the apparatus must be sealed if the mass is to be checked.

options.text: The vessel must be sealed to keep it
Gases have no mass to measure
options.why: Gases have mass, which is why they must be kept.

options.text: Mass is not conserved for gases
options.why: Mass is conserved for gases as for everything else.
Gaseous products form in very many reactions.

2731.stem: A textbook writes H2O without a state symbol in a combustion equation. The most reasonable reading is that
2731.explanation: The author has left the state unspecified because it depends on temperature: steam while hot, liquid once cooled.

options.text: the state is left open deliberately

options.why: Water certainly has a state in any given situation.
A missing state symbol does not affect balance.
Water is a genuine product of combustion.

2731.stem: Which situation would make (s) and (aq) both defensible for the same product?
2731.explanation: A sparingly soluble product such as calcium hydroxide dissolves partly and settles partly, so either symbol can be justified depending on the amount of water.

options.why: A very soluble product is unambiguously aqueous.
A completely insoluble product is unambiguously solid.
A gas is neither solid nor aqueous.

2731.stem: State symbols are sometimes described as the bridge between the equation and the laboratory. The strongest support for this is that they
2731.explanation: They alone tell the reader what apparatus is needed and what will be seen, which is the information a bench chemist acts on.

options.text: say what apparatus and observation to expect
give the masses to weigh out
options.why: Masses come from coefficients and molar masses.
Temperature is written above the arrow if at all.
Only experiment can establish that.

2731.stem: Why would writing (s) for a dissolved ionic salt mislead a student about its behaviour?
2731.explanation: A dissolved salt exists as free ions that can react and conduct electricity, whereas a solid holds its ions locked in a lattice.

options.text: Its ions are free to move and react

options.why: Insoluble solids sit in water unchanged.
Ionic solids are made entirely of ions.
They have formulae like any other substance.

2731.stem: In an examination, an otherwise perfect equation loses a mark for a wrong state symbol. The fairest assessment is that
2731.explanation: The symbol is a chemical claim about what is observed, so getting it wrong is a genuine error rather than a presentational slip.

options.text: the symbol is itself a chemical claim

options.why: The symbol asserts something testable about the reaction.
They carry specific physical meaning.
Balance is one of several things an equation must get right.

2731.stem: What does the existence of four state symbols rather than three tell us about how chemists describe matter?
2731.explanation: Being dissolved is treated as a distinct chemical situation, not merely a physical state, because a dissolved substance behaves differently from the pure liquid.

options.text: Being dissolved is a situation in its own right
There are four states of matter
options.why: The classical states are three; (aq) is about dissolving.
The (g) symbol is used constantly.
They behave very differently, which is why both symbols exist.

2732.stem: Conditions such as heat or a catalyst are written
2732.explanation: Reaction conditions are written above or below the arrow, not as reactants.

options.why: A catalyst is not consumed, so it is not a reactant.
A condition is not formed by the reaction.
Brackets after a formula hold the state symbol.

2732.stem: The Greek letter delta or the word 'heat' above an arrow means the reaction needs
2732.explanation: A delta above the arrow indicates that heating is required for the reaction to proceed.

options.why: Cooling is not indicated by a delta.
Stirring is not shown in a chemical equation.
Filtering is a separation step, not a reaction condition.

2732.stem: A catalyst written above the arrow is a substance that
2732.explanation: A catalyst changes the rate of a reaction without being consumed by it.

options.why: Being consumed is what makes something a reactant.
A catalyst is present at the start and the end.
A catalyst changes the rate, not the products.

2732.stem: In the equation for photosynthesis, the condition written above the arrow is
2732.explanation: Sunlight supplies the energy for photosynthesis and is written above the arrow, often with chlorophyll.

options.why: Photosynthesis requires light, not its absence.
Pressure is not a condition for photosynthesis.
No acid is involved in photosynthesis.

2732.stem: Writing a condition above the arrow rather than as a reactant shows that it
2732.explanation: It is needed for the reaction but is not itself chemically consumed by it.

options.why: A consumed substance is written as a reactant.
A formed substance is written as a product.

2732.stem: In the Haber process, the catalyst written above the arrow is

options.why: Copper is not the catalyst for ammonia synthesis.

2732.stem: A reaction requiring sunlight is described as
2732.explanation: A reaction driven by light is called a photochemical reaction.

options.why: Thermal reactions are driven by heat.
Electrolytic reactions are driven by electricity.
Catalytic describes the use of a catalyst.

2732.stem: Which condition is needed for the decomposition of water into its elements?
2732.explanation: Electrolysis supplies electrical energy, which is what splits water into hydrogen and oxygen.

options.why: Warming water boils it rather than decomposing it.
Sunlight alone does not split liquid water.
Magnetism does not drive chemical decomposition.

2732.stem: In the hydrogenation of vegetable oil, the catalyst is usually
2732.explanation: Nickel is the catalyst used to add hydrogen to unsaturated oils.

options.why: Iron catalyses ammonia synthesis, not hydrogenation.
Zinc is not used as a hydrogenation catalyst.
Lead is not used as a hydrogenation catalyst.

2732.stem: Conditions are worth writing in an equation because they
2732.explanation: Without them the equation looks like a change that would occur on its own, which may be quite untrue.

options.why: Balance depends only on atom counts.
Products are named on the right of the arrow.
Masses come from coefficients and molar masses.

2732.stem: The symbol for heating in a chemical equation is
2732.explanation: A capital Greek delta written above the arrow is the standard symbol for heat.

options.why: A plus sign joins substances on one side.
Brackets after a formula hold the state symbol.

2732.stem: Silver chloride decomposes in the presence of
2732.explanation: Sunlight provides the energy that breaks silver chloride into silver and chlorine.

options.why: Magnetism does not drive chemical decomposition.
Silver chloride is stable in cold water in the dark.
Nitrogen is unreactive and causes no decomposition.

2732.stem: Pressure is written as a condition mainly for reactions involving
2732.explanation: Pressure matters most when gases take part, because it changes how closely gas particles are packed.

options.why: Pressure has very little effect on solids.
Precipitation is barely affected by pressure.
Liquids are nearly incompressible.

2732.stem: If a condition is omitted from an equation, the equation is
2732.explanation: It remains balanced and chemically correct but tells the reader less about how to bring the reaction about.

options.why: Conditions play no part in balancing.
It still uses formulae.
Equations are often written without conditions.

2732.stem: Which equation would most mislead a student if its condition were omitted?
2732.explanation: Photosynthesis appears to happen spontaneously without sunlight and chlorophyll written above the arrow.

options.why: Neutralisation needs no special condition.
Mixing two solutions needs no special condition.

2732.stem: A reaction is written with 'conc. H2SO4' above the arrow. The acid is most likely acting as

options.why: A consumed reactant belongs on the left of the arrow.
A product belongs on the right of the arrow.
State symbols go in brackets after a formula.

2732.stem: Why does writing 'heat' above the arrow differ in meaning from writing 'heat' on the product side?
2732.explanation: Above the arrow it means heat must be supplied; on the product side it means heat is released.

options.text: One means supplied, the other released

options.why: The position reverses the direction of energy flow.
Above the arrow indicates heat being supplied.
On the product side it indicates heat being released.

2732.stem: A student writes nickel as a reactant in the hydrogenation of oil. The correction is that nickel
2732.explanation: Nickel is recovered unchanged, so it belongs above the arrow as a catalyst.

2732.stem: In an industrial equation, both a temperature and a pressure are written above the arrow. This suggests the reaction
2732.explanation: Specified temperature and pressure indicate a gas-phase equilibrium whose yield depends on both.

options.why: Pressure would matter little for a solution reaction.
Such processes very often use a catalyst as well.
Pressure has little effect on solid products.

2732.stem: Which condition would you write above the arrow for the thermal decomposition of limestone?
2732.explanation: Strong heating is required, so a delta or the word heat is written above the arrow.

options.why: Limestone does not decompose in sunlight.
Electrolysis is not used to decompose limestone.
No catalyst is needed for thermal decomposition.

2732.stem: A reaction proceeds at room temperature in the dark. Writing a condition above the arrow would be
2732.explanation: With no special requirement, there is nothing to record and the arrow is left plain.

options.why: Conditions are written only when they are needed.
Conditions play no part in balancing.
Products are named on the right of the arrow.

2732.stem: Which change to an equation would most change the chemistry it describes?
2732.explanation: Moving a catalyst from above the arrow onto the reactant side claims it is consumed, which is a different chemical statement.

options.text: Moving a catalyst to the reactant side

options.why: A state symbol adds information without changing identity.
Order carries no chemical meaning.
The delta is simply a shorter way of writing heat.

2732.stem: Chlorophyll is written above the arrow in photosynthesis because it
2732.explanation: Chlorophyll absorbs light and enables the reaction but is not consumed, so it acts as a catalyst.

options.text: enables the reaction without being used up

options.why: Glucose is built from carbon dioxide and water.
Chlorophyll persists in the leaf after the reaction.
Chlorophyll is present before the reaction begins.

2732.stem: The condition 'in the presence of moisture' in the rusting equation is written as a reactant instead, because water

options.text: is consumed and ends up in the rust

options.why: Water is actually built into the product.
Water is incorporated into hydrated iron oxide.
Iron does not rust at all without water.

2732.stem: Two equations for the same reactants differ in the catalyst written above the arrow, and give different products. This shows a catalyst can

2732.stem: Writing '1atm, 25 C' above an arrow specifies

Rate is not conveyed by an equation.

2732.stem: An equation for a reaction that needs both heat and a catalyst should show
2732.explanation: Both conditions are written around the arrow, conventionally the catalyst above and the temperature below, or both above.

options.why: Omitting the heat hides a genuine requirement.

2732.stem: Why does the position of a substance relative to the arrow carry chemical meaning rather than being a layout choice?
2732.explanation: Position asserts a role: consumed on the left, formed on the right, required but unconsumed above, and those are three different chemical claims.

options.why: Atom counts depend only on what is on each side.
Rate is not conveyed by an equation.
The three positions make three distinct claims.

2732.stem: A student argues that since a catalyst is not consumed it need not be written at all. The strongest counter is that
2732.explanation: Without it the reaction may not proceed at a useful rate, so anyone trying to reproduce the reaction needs to know it is required.

options.text: the reaction may not proceed without it

options.why: Catalysts are genuinely recovered unchanged.

options.text: it is needed to balance the equation
options.why: Catalysts play no part in balancing.

2732.stem: Two industrial equations differ only in the temperature above the arrow, and the yields differ greatly. This is best explained by

2732.stem: Why is 'in sunlight' a more informative condition for silver chloride than 'at room temperature'?

2732.stem: Which claim about conditions is best supported by the fact that the same reactants can give different products?

2732.stem: Why does a student who omits 'electrolysis' from the water decomposition equation risk a serious misunderstanding?

2732.stem: A reaction requires a catalyst only at industrial scale, not in the laboratory. The best way to record this is

That misrepresents the industrial case.

options.text: write it as a reactant instead

2732.stem: What does the practice of writing conditions above the arrow reveal about what a chemical equation is for?
2732.explanation: It is a set of instructions as well as a statement of fact, meant to let another chemist reproduce the change.

options.text: It is a statement about rate

2732.stem: Why can the absence of a condition above an arrow itself be informative?

2732.stem: Why does including conditions make an equation harder to falsify but more useful?
2732.explanation: The equation now claims a specific result under specified circumstances, which is a sharper and more testable claim than a bare list of substances.
